Pool Resurfacing in Phoenix

When the inside of a pool turns rough, stained or flaky, the fix is a new interior finish. Here is how the job works in the Valley, what the finish choices are, and how to check the company before anyone drains the water.

Call (623) 240-0428 Compare the finish types
  1. Home
  2. Services
  3. Pool Resurfacing

Pool resurfacing in Phoenix means stripping or roughening the worn inside layer of a concrete pool and applying a fresh finish over the shell. It is not a cleaning job and not a quick patch. The pool is drained, the old surface is prepared, a new layer of plaster, quartz, pebble or tile goes on, and the pool is refilled and nursed through its first weeks. Done well, it gives the pool a new skin that should last for many seasons. Done in a hurry, it can flake, stain or crack early.

Phoenix Pool Cleaning Pro does not resurface pools. It is a free phone line. Call (623) 240-0428 at any hour, describe what the pool surface looks like, and the call is passed to an independent, locally owned pool company in the Valley. That company inspects the pool, gives you its own quote, does the work and bills you directly. This page is here so you know what to look for, what to ask and how to check the company first.

Signs your pool surface is due

A pool finish wears out slowly, so many owners only notice when someone scrapes a foot or snags a swimsuit. Walk the pool with the water clear and the sun high, and look for these:

  • Rough, sandpaper texture. The smooth top of the finish has worn away, leaving grit that catches skin and fabric.
  • Etching. A pitted, chalky or blotchy look where the surface has been eaten into.
  • Stains that come back. Brown, gray or mottled patches that return soon after a careful cleaning, or that never lift at all.
  • Hollow or flaking areas. Spots that sound hollow when tapped, blister, or peel away in flakes, because the finish has lost its bond to the surface underneath or is splitting apart.
  • Thin or exposed spots. Dark patches where the base coat or the concrete shell is showing through.
  • A web of fine cracks across large areas, rather than one small line in one spot.

One or two of these in a small area may only need a spot repair. When they spread across the floor and walls, a full resurface is usually the honest answer. If you are not sure which side of that line your pool is on, the guide to repairing or resurfacing a pool walks through the decision, and a leak or a crack that keeps growing belongs on the leak and crack repair page first.

Angi's Phoenix resurfacing page points to the same local culprits most owners suspect: intense heat, strong sun, hard water and mineral buildup all wear on a pool's interior here. That is one reason Valley pools seldom go decades without attention.

Pool finish types compared

These are the four interiors most often quoted for a concrete pool. Life spans are as each named source states them, and real results depend on water care. Brand names are left out on purpose: ask the company to explain its product in plain terms.

Pool interior finishes compared by what they are, how they feel and their published life span
FinishWhat it isHow it feels and looksPublished life span
White plasterWhite cement, white marble aggregate and water, troweled smooth over the shellSmooth underfoot, classic light blue water, shows stains and etching sooner than the othersAbout 7 to 12 years (HomeGuide); Angi says up to about 10 years
Quartz aggregatePlaster with colored quartz granules blended inSmooth with a slight texture, comes in many colors, hides minor staining better than plain whiteAbout 10 to 15 years (HomeGuide)
Pebble aggregateSmall smooth stones set in a cement base, then exposed at the surfaceBumpy, natural look, rougher on bare feet than plasterAbout 15 to 20 years or more (HomeGuide)
TileCeramic or glass tile set over the whole interiorSmooth and very durable, the most custom lookUp to 50 years when well kept (Angi, ceramic tile)

Cost tends to climb from left to right in the same order the durability does. Angi's city cost data lists tile at several times the per-square-foot price of plaster, and HomeGuide places pebble above standard plaster. A cheaper finish redone more often is not automatically a bad choice, especially on an older pool that may face other big repairs soon. Ask for prices on two finishes side by side so you can weigh the trade.

How a resurfacing job runs, step by step

Every company has its own routine, but a careful job follows roughly this order. Knowing it helps you read a quote and ask the right questions.

  1. Inspection and written quote. Someone looks at the whole interior, the waterline tile, the coping stones around the edge and the fittings, then puts the scope and price in writing.
  2. Draining. The pool is pumped out. Where that water goes is set by your city, not by the company's habit, so ask how they will handle it under your city's rule before the day arrives.
  3. Prep. Loose and hollow finish is removed, and the remaining surface is chipped, ground or roughened so the new layer can bond. Fittings, lights and drains are protected or reset. The National Plasterers Council names a poor bond between the new finish and the surface under it as a main cause of finish failures, and says loose, delaminated material must be removed, not plastered over.
  4. Repairs found once it is empty. Cracks, a damaged tile line or loose coping often show up only after the water is gone. Any added work should come to you as a written change order that both sides sign before it is done.
  5. Applying the new finish. The crew applies and trowels the new material while it is workable. Timing matters here, which is why the work tends to happen in one long push.
  6. Refilling. Refill timing follows the company's startup plan for the finish; filling too early is one of the mistakes the National Plasterers Council lists. Ask when the fill will start and whether the hose should run without stopping.
  7. Startup and the first weeks. A new cement-based finish releases fine plaster dust in its first weeks. Pool & Hot Tub Alliance startup guidance calls for brushing the whole surface at least twice a day with the filter running until the dust clears, plus careful water balancing. Get that startup routine in writing so you know who does what.

Why draining in the summer heat matters

A drained pool in a Valley summer is a concrete basin sitting in full sun. That shapes the job in a few practical ways, and a good company will raise them before you do.

  • Timing within the day. Ask what time work starts and how the crew keeps the new finish from drying too fast on a hot afternoon.
  • How long the shell sits empty. Every extra day empty is a day of sun on bare surfaces and a day the pool is unusable. Ask for the expected number of days from drain to refill.
  • Dust and storms. Summer storms can blow dirt, leaves and grit into an empty or freshly filled pool. Ask how the company protects fresh work if a storm rolls in.
  • Refill water. Filling a pool takes a lot of tap water, and Valley water is hard. Ask how the company will balance the fresh fill so it does not start scaling or etching the new surface.
  • Safety. An empty pool is a long fall onto concrete. Keep children and pets out of the yard while it is drained, and keep any gate latched.

Some owners prefer to schedule the job in the cooler months for these reasons. Whatever the season, the questions above are worth asking.

What a pool resurfacing quote should list

A one-line price on a business card is not a quote. Before you agree to resurfacing, the written estimate should spell out:

  • The finish type, color and thickness, in plain words.
  • How the old surface will be prepared, and whether any of it is being fully removed.
  • Draining and refilling: who does it, and where the drained water will go.
  • What happens with the waterline tile, coping, lights, steps and fittings: kept, cleaned, reset or replaced.
  • How hidden repairs will be priced and approved, ideally with a signed change order.
  • The startup routine after refill and who carries it out.
  • The payment schedule. The Registrar of Contractors advises not letting payments get ahead of the work.
  • The company's name exactly as it appears on its ROC license, and the license number.
  • Any written workmanship or materials warranty, with what it covers and for how long.

The ROC also suggests getting written estimates from at least three contractors and checking that the contract matches the estimate before you sign. Our guide to choosing a pool company in Phoenix covers contracts, reviews and red flags in more depth.

Licensing: who may replace a pool finish in Arizona

Arizona's Registrar of Contractors (ROC) sorts contractors into license classifications. Its residential R-6 Swimming Pool Service and Repair license allows servicing and minor repair of residential pools. The ROC states plainly that R-6 does not allow a complete replacement of plaster or pebble pool interiors and decks. A full resurface needs a contractor whose license covers that scope, such as the residential B-5 swimming pool contractor classification, which the ROC describes as building and repairing pools and spas.

So the useful question is not just "are you licensed?" but "which classification do you hold, and does it cover a full resurface?" Look the number up on the ROC search and read the classification listed. If the answer is unclear, the ROC can tell you which license fits the job.

Check the license first. Arizona's Registrar of Contractors (ROC) licenses contractors, and its residential classifications include R-6, Swimming Pool Service and Repair. Repairs, equipment replacement and resurfacing generally call for a licensed contractor; whether a cleaning-only service needs a license is not spelled out, so ask the ROC if it matters to you. Ask the company for its ROC license number and look it up on the ROC contractor search (opens in a new tab) before work begins. The line does not check this for you.

Pool deck repair and resurfacing in Phoenix

The deck around a pool takes the same sun as the water and usually more foot traffic. Cracked, flaking or hot, faded coatings are common reasons owners ask about deck work while the pool is being redone. Some pool companies also coat or repair decks; others focus only on the interior and refer the deck out. Either way, the deck should be its own line on the quote. Keep in mind that the R-6 service and repair license does not allow a complete replacement of decks, so ask what license covers the deck portion as well.

Pool resurfacing in Phoenix: published cost figures

Angi's Phoenix pool resurfacing page gives an average of about $11,363, with most homeowners in the city spending roughly $6,198 to $15,495. HomeGuide's national 2026 figures, based on about 1,000 square feet of surface, put a standard plaster job at about $6,000 to $8,000, a quartz plaster job at about $7,000 to $10,000 and pebble at about $7,000 to $15,000. Both are third-party estimates rather than anything this line charges, and real Phoenix quotes vary widely.

What moves the number:

  • Pool size and shape. More square feet of floor, wall, steps and benches means more material and labor.
  • The finish. Pebble and tile generally cost more than plaster.
  • Prep. A full removal of the old finish costs more than roughening a sound surface.
  • Extras. New waterline tile, coping, lights or crack repairs found once the pool is empty.
  • Deck work, if it is added to the same project.

For how resurfacing fits alongside routine service costs, see our guide to pool service cost in Phoenix.

Keeping a new finish looking new

Most of what shortens a finish happens in the water, not on the trowel. Water that is out of balance can slowly dissolve a cement-based surface or coat it in scale. Regular testing and brushing, and a filter that is kept clean, do more for a new surface than any product. The pool cleaning and weekly maintenance page explains the routine, and pool tile cleaning covers the white calcium line that forms at the waterline in the Valley.

Common questions

How much does pool resurfacing cost in Phoenix?

Angi's Phoenix cost page gives an average of about $11,363, with most homeowners in the city spending roughly $6,198 to $15,495. HomeGuide's national guide puts a standard plaster job at about $6,000 to $8,000 and pebble at about $7,000 to $15,000. Those figures come from the named guides; this line sets no prices. The size of the pool, the finish, the prep and any repairs found once the pool is empty all move the number, so the written quote from the company that sees your pool is the one that counts.

Do pool resurfacing companies need a license in Arizona?

Generally, yes. The Arizona Registrar of Contractors says its R-6 Swimming Pool Service and Repair license covers service and minor repair, and it does not allow a complete replacement of plaster or pebble pool interiors and decks. A full resurface therefore calls for a contractor whose classification covers it, such as the B-5 swimming pool contractor license. Ask for the license number and look it up on the ROC contractor search before you sign. The line does not check licenses for you.

Which pool finish lasts the longest?

Of the common finishes, tile lasts longest: Angi says a well-kept ceramic tile interior can last up to 50 years. HomeGuide lists pebble at about 15 to 20 years or more, quartz at about 10 to 15 years and standard plaster at about 7 to 12 years. Real life in the Valley depends heavily on water chemistry and care, so treat those spans as a guide, not a promise.

Can the pool deck be resurfaced at the same time?

Often it can be planned alongside, but it is a separate piece of work with its own line on the quote. Some companies coat or repair decks and some do not. The ROC's R-6 service and repair license does not allow a complete replacement of decks either, so ask which license covers the deck work and check it on the ROC search.

Where does the water go when the pool is drained for resurfacing?

Each Valley city sets its own rule on where drained pool water may go. Before the pump goes in, ask the company where the water will be sent and how that follows your city's rule, and read your city's water or stormwater page if you are unsure. Our guide on draining a pool in Arizona has more on the water side.
